# Results — Study 234 (Olympic-Year) on real ^GSPC data

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Source: yfinance ^GSPC
daily prices, December-close used to compute calendar-year log-returns.
Calendar years 1928–2024 (n = 97 annual returns).
As-of **2026-06-16**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n years | Fingerprint (ret_pct col) |
|---|---|---|---|
| yfinance ^GSPC | 1928–2024 | 97 | `b725f3543071` |

*Olympic years in sample (n = 23): 1928, 1932, 1936, 1948, 1952, 1956, 1960, 1964,
1968, 1972, 1976, 1980, 1984, 1988, 1992, 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020,
2024.  Non-Olympic years: n = 74.  Note: 2020 Tokyo games were held in 2021 (COVID
postponement); we use the scheduled year (2020).*

## Olympic vs non-Olympic — mean calendar-year return

| Group | n | Mean % | Std % |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Non-Olympic | 74 | +7.74 | 19.99 |
| **Olympic** | **23** | **+8.89** | **15.96** |
| Grand mean | 97 | +8.01 | 18.93 |

The raw Olympic-year mean (+8.89%) is slightly above the non-Olympic mean (+7.74%),
but the difference is **+1.15 pp** — well inside one standard error.

## Olympic contrast and HAC inference

| Measure | Value |
|---|--:|
| Olympic-year mean | **+8.89%** |
| Non-Olympic-year mean | +7.74% |
| Contrast (Olympic minus Non-Olympic) | **+1.15 pp** |
| Grand mean | +8.01% |
| HAC t-stat (Newey-West, Olympic vs grand mean) | **+0.29** |
| SE | 3.00 pp |
| n (Olympic years) | 23 |
| Low-power warning | YES — n=23 Olympic observations |

The HAC t-stat of **+0.29** is nowhere near the |t| ≥ 2 bar.  The contrast of
+1.15 pp is less than 0.4 standard errors and is entirely consistent with sampling
noise.  The sign is positive, but noise easily produces such a small difference in
any 23-observation sub-sample of a 97-year series.

## Permutation test

50,000 random relabellings of the Olympic flag across the 97 years:

| Test | p-value |
|---|--:|
| |contrast| ≥ observed (+1.15 pp), **two-sided** | **0.803** |
| contrast ≥ observed (+1.15 pp), one-sided | 0.407 |

A two-sided p of **0.80** means 80% of random labellings produce a contrast at
least this large in absolute value — the observed gap is well within the bulk of the
null distribution.  The one-sided p of 0.41 is equally uninformative.  There is no
detectable Olympic-year effect.

## Pre/post 1972 split (Bretton Woods break)

| Period | n (Olympic) | Olympic mean | Non-Olympic mean | Contrast |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Pre-1972 (1928–1971) | 9 | +9.16% | +5.63% | **+3.53 pp** |
| Post-1972 (1972–2024) | 14 | +8.71% | +9.64% | **−0.92 pp** |

The pre-1972 contrast looks modestly positive (+3.5 pp), but the post-1972 contrast
reverses sign (−0.9 pp).  With n = 9 and n = 14 in each half, neither sub-period
has enough power to distinguish a real effect from noise.  The reversal is itself
evidence against a persistent mechanism.

## Could you trade it? Olympic timing strategy

Hold S&P 500 only in Olympic years; sit in cash in all other years:

| Strategy | Annualised return |
|---|--:|
| Buy-and-hold (1928–2024) | **+6.17%/yr** |
| Olympic-only (in cash 74 of 97 years) | **+1.75%/yr** |
| Annual advantage | **−4.42%/yr** |

The "Olympic-only" strategy is a disaster — you are in cash three years out of four,
missing most of the equity premium.  This is a reductio ad absurdum of the timing
logic: even if Olympic years were slightly better than average, being out of the
market 76% of the time destroys compounding.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** HAC t = +0.29; two-sided permutation p = 0.80.  Olympic years
  average +1.15 pp more than non-Olympic years, which is statistically
  indistinguishable from zero in a 97-year series with 23 Olympic events.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The Olympic-year timing strategy yields +1.75%/yr
  vs +6.17%/yr for buy-and-hold, a −4.42%/yr penalty from being in cash most of
  the time.  Even ignoring the absent signal, the strategy is structurally
  unworkable.
- **Myth-check — BUSTED.** The raw mean difference is positive but tiny,
  not statistically significant, reverses sign post-1972, and has no proposed
  causal mechanism.  The Olympic calendar effect is pure numerical folklore.
